clinicalPearls: The most common paratesticular malignancy of childhood and adolescence, arising from mesenchymal tissue of the spermatic cord, epididymis and testicular tunics.
Typically presents as a painless, firm, rapidly enlarging unilateral scrotal or inguinal mass, usually felt separate from and above the testis.
Embryonal histology, including the favourable spindle cell variant, predominates; the alveolar subtype, associated with FOXO1 gene fusions, is more aggressive.
The paratesticular location is classified as a favourable site in rhabdomyosarcoma risk stratification.
Lymphatic drainage follows the gonadal vessels to the retroperitoneal para-aortic and paracaval nodes, so staging of the retroperitoneum is essential.
Adolescents have a substantially higher rate of retroperitoneal nodal involvement and worse outcomes than young children, and warrant more thorough nodal evaluation.
Radical inguinal orchidectomy with high ligation of the spermatic cord is the correct surgical approach; a trans-scrotal approach is avoided.
Treatment is multimodal, combining surgery with chemotherapy and, in selected cases, radiotherapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant tumour of skeletal-muscle lineage that arises from primitive mesenchymal cells retaining the capacity for myogenic (rhabdomyoblastic) differentiation, even at sites such as the paratesticular region where mature skeletal muscle is absent. Embryonal tumours, the commonest subtype at this site, typically show loss of heterozygosity at chromosome 11p15.5 and lack a defining gene fusion, whereas alveolar tumours are characterised by PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 fusions that drive a more aggressive phenotype. Tumour cells express myogenic markers such as desmin, myogenin and MyoD1, which underpin the histological diagnosis. The paratesticular tissues drain via lymphatics accompanying the gonadal vessels to the retroperitoneal para-aortic and paracaval nodes, and this drainage pattern dictates both the risk of nodal spread and the staging and surgical strategy.
additionalDifferentials: Benign paratesticular tumours such as adenomatoid tumour, lipoma or leiomyoma of the cord
Other paratesticular sarcomas such as liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma, which are more typical in adults
additionalInvestigations: Serum tumour markers (alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin and lactate dehydrogenase) to help exclude a germ cell tumour
Radical inguinal orchidectomy specimen for histology and immunohistochemistry (desmin, myogenin, MyoD1)
Molecular testing for FOXO1 gene fusion to distinguish alveolar from embryonal subtype
Cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis for nodal and metastatic staging
MRI of the primary site and pelvis
Bone marrow examination and bone or metabolic imaging in higher-risk or metastatic disease
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging solid scrotal mass in a child or adolescent
Palpable abdominal mass or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy
Prior trans-scrotal biopsy or surgery, which compromises staging and lymphatic drainage
Systemic symptoms or respiratory features suggesting metastatic disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable, particularly for localised embryonal tumours in young children treated with multimodal therapy. Outcomes are worse with the alveolar subtype, nodal or metastatic disease, and in adolescents.
pitfalls: Performing a trans-scrotal biopsy or orchidectomy (scrotal violation), which alters lymphatic drainage, worsens staging and may necessitate hemiscrotectomy
Underestimating retroperitoneal nodal risk in adolescents
Mistaking the mass for epididymo-orchitis and delaying diagnosis with antibiotics
Failing to send tissue for molecular fusion testing
Inadequate cord ligation leaving positive surgical margins
references: Paediatric soft tissue sarcoma cooperative group protocols
European paediatric soft tissue sarcoma study group guidance
Paediatric oncology and urology reference texts
management: Perform radical inguinal orchidectomy with high ligation of the spermatic cord as the primary surgical treatment, avoiding a trans-scrotal approach that risks tumour spillage
Deliver multi-agent systemic chemotherapy with vincristine, actinomycin D and cyclophosphamide as the backbone of multimodal therapy
Stratify treatment intensity by histology and fusion status, escalating for alveolar, FOXO1-fusion-positive tumours which behave more aggressively
Evaluate and stage the retroperitoneal para-aortic and paracaval nodes, with ipsilateral retroperitoneal lymph node dissection especially in adolescents given their higher rate of nodal involvement
Add radiotherapy to the primary site or involved nodes according to risk group and residual disease
Offer sperm banking or other fertility preservation before gonadotoxic chemotherapy or radiotherapy where age-appropriate
Manage within a paediatric and adolescent sarcoma multidisciplinary team, with structured surveillance imaging for local, nodal and pulmonary recurrence
